claims.text: A conventional low-alloy tempered martensitic steel can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition as temperature is varied.
The proposed initial material is susceptible to temper embrittlement through impurity segregation.
Impurity segregation at prior-austenite grain boundaries reaches an embrittling threshold at intermediate temperatures.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation weakens boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion causes brittle behavior and a dramatic loss of ductility.
At lower temperatures, insufficient impurity segregation preserves or restores ductility.
At higher temperatures, re-dissolution or redistribution of impurities restores ductility.
Ductility will be high at low and high temperatures and dramatically lower within a narrow intermediate-temperature window.
Impurity segregation is minimal or absent outside the critical temperature window.
The proposed transition is specific to conventional low-alloy steels that permit impurity segregation.
The transition is not anticipated in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloy systems.
The embrittlement temperature range and magnitude may vary with alloy composition, impurity levels, and experimental conditions.
